title: The three components and the architecture labels
brief: Name each of the three fundamental DSS components, then finish the acronyms from the typical architecture diagram.
hint: Data is stored, models are manipulated, and the dialog is what you interact with. The other four lines are straight from the architecture slide.

blanks.explanation: The data management component stores information from an organisation's traditional data repositories, from external sources such as the Internet, and from the personal insights of individual users.
The model management component handles representations of events, facts or situations; the chapter's two named model kinds are optimisation and goal-seeking.
The user interface management component, or dialog, is what allows a user to interact with the system. In the three-letter form it is the DGMS.
TPS is the transaction processing system: the operational source that feeds current data into the DSS database.
OLAP is on-line analytical processing, and it provides the highest level of functionality in a data-driven DSS.
The slide defines the DSS database as current data from applications or groups.
Data mining is the technology for finding relationships in large databases for prediction.

steps: Chapter 1 names exactly three fundamental components: the database management system (DBMS), the model management system (MBMS) and the dialog generation and management system (DGMS). The first two blanks are data and model; the dialog is the third.

Read the descriptions back. Storing information from internal repositories, the Internet and users' insights is data management. Representations of events, facts or situations built as optimisation or goal-seeking models is model management. Allowing the user to interact is the user interface management component.

The architecture diagram then labels the boxes around those three. TPS supplies the transaction data, OLAP is on-line analytical processing, and the DSS database holds current data from applications or groups.
Data mining sits in the same diagram as the prediction tool: it finds relationships in large databases rather than storing models or printing reports.

title: Characteristic or limitation?
brief: Mark each statement as one of the chapter's DSS characteristics or one of its stated limitations.
hint: Three of these are the limitation slide: what a DSS cannot do, what its interface cannot yet parse, and what a narrow scope prevents.

blanks.explanation: Support for decision makers in semi-structured and unstructured problems is item 1 of the characteristics list.
Supporting managers at all levels is item 2 of the characteristics list.
The limitation slide says language and command interfaces are not yet sophisticated enough to allow natural language processing of user directives and inquiries.
Effectiveness, but not efficiency, is listed as a capability: the decision's quality counts, not the system's speed.
Complete control by decision-makers is item 5 of the characteristics list.
Being designed to a narrow scope of application, which inhibits generalisability to multiple decision contexts, is the third stated limitation.
A DSS cannot be designed to contain distinctly human decision making such as creativity, imagination or intuition.
Adaptability and flexibility, plus ease of development by end users, both appear in the characteristics list.

steps: Split the slide deck in your head first: Chapter 1 has one list of characteristics and capabilities, and one separate slide titled Limitations of DSS.

The limitations list has exactly three entries: no creativity, imagination or intuition; no natural-language processing of user directives; and a narrow scope that blocks generalisability. Blanks 3, 6 and 7 are those three, so mark them limitation.

Everything else quoted here comes from the characteristics list: semi-structured and unstructured support, all management levels, individuals and groups, interdependent or sequential decisions, complete control by decision-makers, and effectiveness but not efficiency.
Adaptability, flexibility and ease of development by end users appear in the second half of the characteristics list, so blank 8 is a characteristic too.

title: Sort six scenarios into Power's five types
brief: For each scenario, pick the DSS type that Power (2002) assigns it, using the mode of assistance as the criterion.
hint: Ask what the system actually assists with: a model, a dataset, a document, expertise in rules, or people talking to each other.

blanks.explanation: Knowledge-driven DSS provide specialised problem-solving expertise stored as facts, rules or procedures and recommend actions. MYCIN is the chapter's example.
A spreadsheet with formulas is the first example listed under model-driven DSS: the user manipulates a model with parameters.
Communication-driven DSS use network and communication technologies to support more than one person on a shared task; video conferencing is the listed example.
Emphasis on access to and manipulation of a time series of internal company data is the data-driven definition.
Document-driven DSS manage, retrieve and manipulate unstructured information such as scanned documents, hypertext, images, sound and video, with a search engine as the primary tool.
An optimum routing model is model-driven, and the chapter notes model-driven DSS are not necessarily data intensive.

steps: Power's criterion is the mode of assistance, so classify by what the user is handed: a rule base, a model, a document store, a dataset, or a network.
Rules that recommend a diagnosis mean expertise has been stored as facts and rules, which is knowledge-driven.
Formulas, forecasting models and routing models are all models the user manipulates with parameters, so blanks 2 and 6 are model-driven.

A decade of internal sales figures is a time series of company data, which is the data-driven family; scanned reports, images and video are unstructured documents, which is the document-driven family.
People collaborating on a shared task over network technology is communication-driven, and the chapter adds that this type is related to group decision support systems.

The distinguishing sentence about the model-driven family is that it uses user-supplied data and parameters and is not necessarily data intensive, so blank 3 is intensive.

The functionality ladder for the data-driven family is stated in ascending order: simple file systems accessed by query and retrieval tools, then data warehouses for additional functionality, then OLAP at the top.
That leaves query for blank 4, data for blank 5 and OLAP for blank 6.

title: Structured, semi-structured or unstructured
brief: Label each decision with the category the chapter's examples place it in.
hint: Routine and repetitive with a standard solution is structured. Judgment alone on a fuzzy problem is unstructured. Anything mixing the two is semi-structured.

blanks.explanation: Warehouse distribution is on the structured list: routine, repetitive and predictable with a standard solution.
Inventory control is a semi-structured example: a standard procedure plus individual judgment.
Executive recruiting is listed as unstructured, relying on intuition and judgment with no cut-and-dried solution.
Point of sales is a structured example, handled by transaction processing.
Credit evaluation is the classic semi-structured case: rules narrow the field, a person decides the rest.
Research and development planning is listed as unstructured, at the strategic end.
Negotiation appears in the unstructured row under managerial control.
Quality assurance is listed with inventory control and credit evaluation as semi-structured.

steps: Use the chapter's own three tests. Structured decisions are routine and repetitive, objectives are clearly defined in all phases, and standard solutions exist.

Unstructured decisions are non-routine, unpredictable and fuzzy, have no cut-and-dried solution, and apply intuition and judgment through the intelligence, design and choice phases of the Simon model.
Semi-structured is the mix: non-routine but predictable, requiring standard solution procedures together with individual judgment.

Applying that: warehouse distribution and point of sales are structured; recruiting an executive, R&D planning and negotiation are unstructured; inventory control, credit evaluation and quality assurance are the semi-structured three.

title: Which system, which era, which level
brief: Place each information system on the timeline, then finish the two lines about management levels.
hint: Four systems, four dates: early 1960s, the 1960s, early 1970s, late 1980s. The later and more interactive the system, the higher the management level it serves.
code:
Complete the information-system timeline.

  {{1}}  early 1960s, operational, routine transactions
  {{2}}  the 1960s, summary and exception reports
  {{3}}  early 1970s, semi and unstructured problems
  {{4}}  late 1980s, senior level, graphics, drill-down

  The three levels are strategic, {{5}} and operational.
  A DSS was originally built for {{6}} management.

blanks.explanation: Transaction Processing Systems were developed in the early 1960s, serve the operational level, and perform and record daily routine and repetitive transactions.
Management Information Systems came in the 1960s, serve operational or middle management, and produce summary and exception reports.
Decision Support Systems were developed in the early 1970s with a primary focus on semi-structured and unstructured decision making.
Executive Information Systems, also called Executive Support Systems, came in the late 1980s for senior management, with graphics and drill-down.
The three levels of management activity are strategic, tactical and operational.
The chapter says a DSS was originally designed to serve the middle management level, even though its characteristics list later says it supports managers at all levels.

steps: Order the four systems by date, not by importance: TPS early 1960s, MIS the 1960s, DSS early 1970s, EIS late 1980s.
Then check each against the level it serves: operational for TPS, operational or middle for MIS, middle for the original DSS, senior for EIS.

The focus tells them apart as well. TPS is structured decision making, MIS is fairly structured with summary and exception reports, DSS is semi-structured and unstructured, and EIS monitors organisational performance for executives.
The last two blanks come from the same slide: the three levels of management activity are strategic, tactical and operational, and the DSS was originally aimed at middle management.

title: Data subsystem or model subsystem?
brief: The parts and the general functions of the two management subsystems, each labelled as data management or model management.
hint: Anything that stores, describes or retrieves data, or protects it, is on the data side; anything that stores, builds, lists or runs models is on the model side.

blanks.explanation: The DSS database is the first of the four parts listed for the data management subsystem.
The data directory is the third part of the data management subsystem; its model-side twin is the model directory.
The query facility is the fourth part of the data management subsystem: it is how the user gets data out.
The model base stores and organises the various models the DSS uses in its analyses, and it is the modelling counterpart of the database.
The model directory is one of the five parts the chapter lists for the model management subsystem.
The modelling language both appears as a part of the model management subsystem and heads the list of MBMS general functions, because it allows the creation of decision models.
Data integrity is one of the six general functions of the DBMS: the user describes rules that maintain integrity and check for errors.
Transaction recovery is a DBMS function: mechanisms for restart and reconciliation in the event of hardware failure.
The model library is an MBMS function: it stores and manages all the models and provides a catalogue and description of them.

blanks.placeholder: one word
blanks.explanation: The chapter titles the model management subsystem as the analog of the database management subsystem, and Marakas calls the MBMS the counterpart to the DBMS.

steps: The two subsystems are deliberately parallel, so learn them as pairs rather than as two unrelated lists.

Blanks 1 to 3 are data-side parts: the DSS database, the database management system, the data directory and the query facility, and blanks 4 to 6 are model-side parts, where the model base answers the database and the model directory answers the data directory.

The function rows split the same way. Data integrity and transaction recovery belong to the DBMS with data definition, data manipulation, access control and concurrency control, which is six functions in all.

The model library belongs to the MBMS, which has only three general functions: the modelling language, the model library itself, and model manipulation with run, store and query functions similar to those in a DBMS.
The closing pair of lines carries the two lines examiners like: the model base is what differentiates a DSS from other information systems, and the MBMS is the analog of the DBMS.

title: From file systems to warehouses to OLAP
brief: The ascending data-oriented functionality ladder, what a data warehouse holds, and the five listed styles of business intelligence.
hint: The ladder runs from the plainest storage to the most analytical. The warehouse rows use the chapter's own originally and today contrast.

    {{3}}                the highest level

blanks.placeholder: one word
blanks.explanation: Simple file systems accessed by query and retrieval tools give the elementary level of data-oriented functionality.

blanks.placeholder: one word
blanks.explanation: Data warehouses are the middle rung, adding functionality above plain files.

blanks.placeholder: abbreviation
blanks.explanation: OLAP, Online Analytical Processing, provides the highest level and lets users analyse data from many business perspectives.
The slide says a warehouse originally included historical data that were organised and summarised so end users could easily view or manipulate them.
Today some data warehouses include current data as well, which is what lets them support decisions as they happen.
The stated payoff of holding current data as well is real time decision support, which is why the warehouse had to stop being a purely historical store.
The first listed style of BI is report delivery and alerting.

blanks.placeholder: three words
blanks.explanation: The slide glosses cube analysis as slice and dice analysis.

blanks.placeholder: one word
blanks.explanation: Ad-hoc query is the fourth style, and it is what a data-oriented DSS supports alongside ad-hoc reporting.

steps: Read the first block as a ladder of analytical power, not of storage size: plain file systems at the bottom, data warehouses in the middle, OLAP at the top.

The warehouse block is the chapter's originally and today contrast. It originally held organised and summarised historical data for end users, and some warehouses now also carry current data, which is what makes real-time decision support possible.
Data mining sits on top of that store rather than replacing it: the chapter defines it as searching large databases or data warehouses for unknown relationships using intelligent tools.

The five BI styles run from push reporting at one end to statistics and data mining at the other, with enterprise reporting bringing the dashboard and the scorecard and cube analysis bringing the slice and dice view.
Ad-hoc query in style four matches the chapter's one-line definition of a data-oriented DSS, which supports ad-hoc reporting and queries.

title: Fill in the four decision styles
brief: The chapter's four decision style categories as a filled-in note, giving each style its tolerance for ambiguity and the other traits the slides name.
hint: Directive and Analytical are the two the slides contrast on information; Conceptual is the people person and Behavioral avoids conflict.
code:

need for problem {{1}}, and decisions of a
{{2}} nature that require little {{3}}.

blanks.explanation: The directive style combines a low tolerance for ambiguity with a high need for problem structure.
The slide adds that for the directive style these are often decisions of a technical nature.
Directive decisions of a technical nature are the ones that require little information.
Analytical is defined by a greater tolerance for ambiguity than the directive style shows.
The analytical style tends to need more information, which is the opposite of the directive style.
Conceptual has a high tolerance for ambiguity, the same end of the scale as analytical.

blanks.placeholder: what kind of people person?
blanks.explanation: The slide's own phrase for the conceptual style is that it tends to be more a people person.

blanks.placeholder: a low ___ of data
blanks.explanation: Behavioral requires a low amount of data; the slide gives it no tolerance for ambiguity of its own.

blanks.placeholder: what kind of vision
blanks.explanation: The behavioral style demonstrates relatively short-range vision, and is conflict-averse and relies on consensus.

steps: The four styles are separated on two axes, the tolerance for ambiguity and how much information each one needs, so read each block as a pair of answers.
Directive is the tightest of them, with a low tolerance for ambiguity, a high need for problem structure, and decisions of a technical nature that require little information.
Analytical takes the greater tolerance for ambiguity and answers it by needing more information, which is why the design slide asks for access to many data sources for that type.

Conceptual shares the high tolerance for ambiguity but tends to be more a people person, while behavioral is given a low amount of data, relatively short-range vision, and a conflict-averse reliance on consensus, with no ambiguity tolerance stated for it.

The closing two lines are the chapter's design rule: the key issues are the decision maker's reaction to stress and the method in which problems are usually solved, so a directive type who does not handle stress well needs an interface that allows control of the system without tedious input.

brief: The chapter's test of a good decision, the six natures of the forces acting upon the decision maker, and three of the supports a DSS gives.
hint: The forces come in two rows of three in the slides: personal, emotional and economic, then contextual, emergent and organizational.

    attainment of the {{1}} within the
    {{2}} imposed
    the decision maker must {{3}} the forces
    acting upon the process and contend with
    their {{4}}

  SIX NATURES OF THE FORCES
    upper row  personal, {{5}}, economic
    lower row  {{6}}, emergent, {{7}}

  SUPPORT A DSS GIVES

blanks.placeholder: attainment of what?
blanks.explanation: Section 3.3 says a good decision results in attainment of the objective, so the objective is what the decision is measured against.

blanks.placeholder: what is imposed on the decision?
blanks.explanation: The attainment must happen within the constraints imposed, which is what separates the chapter's test from a measure of speed.
Most decision models suggest the decision maker must balance the forces acting upon the process; they are not something that can be removed.

blanks.placeholder: what must be contended with?
blanks.explanation: The same sentence adds that the decision maker must contend with the dynamics of those forces.

blanks.placeholder: a nature of the forces
blanks.explanation: Emotional is the second nature listed, beside personal and economic.

blanks.placeholder: the first nature of the lower row
blanks.explanation: Contextual opens the lower row of three, ahead of emergent and organizational.

blanks.explanation: Organizational closes the list of six natures the chapter gives for the forces acting upon the decision.

blanks.explanation: The support list says a DSS generates multiple and higher quality alternatives, which is what feeds the choice of an option.

steps: The first block is the definition of effectiveness: a good decision results in attainment of the objective within the constraints imposed, so the constraints rather than the clock set the test.
The next three lines explain why that test is hard, because most decision models suggest the decision maker must balance the forces acting upon the process and contend with the dynamics of them.
Those forces come as six natures arranged on the slide as two rows of three, personal, emotional and economic, then contextual, emergent and organizational.
The support block returns to section 3.4, where the DSS generates multiple and higher quality alternatives, provides guidance and reduction of bias, and discourages premature decision-making.

Read together the note gives the chain the chapter builds, a decision maker under pressure from six kinds of force, served by a DSS that widens the options and holds the decision maker back from deciding too early.

title: Name the four stages and their jobs
brief: Simon's model as the chapter stages it, with each stage named, the job it does filled in, and the loop-back the slides attach to it.
hint: The order of the rows is the order of the stages: identify, then develop, then choose, then carry out.

blanks.explanation: Stage 1 is intelligence, the phase in which the decision maker looks for indications that a problem exists and examines the organization's environment for conditions that need decisions.

blanks.placeholder: one verb: what stage 1 does with problems and opportunities
blanks.explanation: The chapter's wording for stage 1 is to identify the problems or opportunities and then collect data or information.

blanks.placeholder: what is collected besides data
blanks.explanation: Data is collected from a variety of sources and processed; the pair the slides use throughout is data or information.
Stage 2 is design, where alternatives are formulated and analyzed, the criteria are defined and possible solutions are tested for feasibility.

blanks.placeholder: possible solutions are analysed or developed for what?
blanks.reveal: analyse or develop the possible solutions for feasibility
blanks.explanation: The design stage line reads analyse or develop the possible solutions for the feasibility, and the testing of solutions for feasibility is repeated in the design-phase slide.
Stage 3 is choice, the phase in which an alternative is selected, the best and most effective course of action from the practical alternatives.

blanks.placeholder: go back to stage 1 or 2 if no solution is what?
blanks.explanation: The chapter's condition for returning from choice is that there are no satisfactory solutions, so the loop-back word is satisfactory.
Stage 4 is implementation, added as the fourth phase, in which the organization devises a plan, obtains the resources and puts the recommended solution to work.

steps: Simon proposed a three-phase model of problem solving, intelligence, design and choice, and the chapter adds implementation as the fourth phase, so the four rows are in the order the slides give them.
Intelligence is the initial phase of problem definition: identify the problems or opportunities, then collect data or information from a variety of sources and process it.

Design analyses or develops the possible solutions for feasibility, defining the criteria, generating alternatives and defining the associations between criteria and alternatives; if the data proves insufficient the chapter sends you back to stage 1.
Choice selects one alternative from the practical ones, and the loop-back is to stage 1 or 2 when there are no satisfactory solutions; a DSS is said to be particularly useful in this stage.

Implementation puts the selected alternative to work, obtaining the resources and dealing with resistance to change, top management support and user training, and a failure of implementation sends the decision maker back to stage 1, 2 or 3.

title: Match the four heuristic biases to their traps
brief: The four major categories of heuristic bias from section 4.6, each paired with the trap the chapter says it produces.
hint: Availability looks back at past experience, anchoring starts from a value, representativeness is about group membership, motivational is about incentives.

blanks.explanation: Availability is the first of the four bias categories, the one that works from past experience.

blanks.placeholder: what do people tend to estimate?
blanks.reveal: people estimate probability from past experience
blanks.explanation: The slide says people tend to estimate probability based on past experience, so probability is what the bias distorts.

blanks.placeholder: the past experience may not be what?
blanks.explanation: The trap the chapter names for availability is that the past experience may not be representative.
The second category is adjustment and anchoring, where a starting value is fixed and then adjusted from.

blanks.placeholder: what kind of value do people pick first?
blanks.explanation: People often pick a starting value and then adjust up and down from it, which is the anchoring half of the category.

blanks.placeholder: what do people underestimate the need for?
blanks.explanation: The slide closes the category by saying people tend to underestimate the need for adjustments.
Representativeness is the third category, the one the chapter defines in terms of group membership.

blanks.placeholder: misestimate the probabilities of what to a group?
blanks.reveal: misestimate the probabilities of belonging to a group
blanks.explanation: The chapter's wording is that people tend to misestimate probabilities of belonging to a group.
Motivational is the fourth category, the one driven by incentives rather than by experience or group membership.

blanks.placeholder: what leads decision makers to restate their estimates?
blanks.reveal: Incentives often lead decision makers to estimate
blanks.explanation: The slide says incentives often lead decision makers to estimate probabilities that do not reflect their true beliefs.

steps: Heuristics are the rules of thumb everyone relies on, and the chapter grants that they are simple to understand, easy to implement, need less conception time and less cognitive effort, and can produce multiple solutions, with searches often landing very close to an exhaustive search.
Because heuristics can also hamper finding a solution, the slides group the traps into four major categories of bias, and each row of this table is one of them.

Availability estimates probability from past experience that may not be representative, while adjustment and anchoring fixes a starting value, adjusts up and down from it and underestimates the need for adjustments.
Representativeness is narrower than it sounds: it is misestimating the probabilities of belonging to a group, not misremembering a past case.

Motivational bias is the one where incentives lead decision makers to put probabilities that do not reflect their true beliefs, so the last row is about who is paying for the answer rather than about what was seen before.

title: Fill the EMV branches of a decision tree
brief: A decision tree for launching through an online channel or a retail store: the payoffs of each state of demand, the probability-weighted terms, the EMV of each branch, the alternative the expected value selects, and the expected value of perfect information.
hint: Each weighted term is the payoff of that state multiplied by the probability of that state, and the three probabilities must total 1.

blanks.placeholder: the probability of low demand
blanks.explanation: The three states of demand form a complete set of outcomes, so low demand carries 1 - 0.5 - 0.3 = 0.2, because the total probability of a complete set must equal 1.

blanks.placeholder: the weighted low-demand term of the online branch
blanks.explanation: Risk analysis weights every outcome by its probability: 0.2 x 50 = 10, next to 0.5 x 120 = 60 and 0.3 x 200 = 60.

blanks.placeholder: the EMV of the online branch
blanks.explanation: Adding the weighted terms gives the expected value of the online branch: 10 + 60 + 60 = RM130,000.

blanks.placeholder: the weighted medium-demand term of the retail branch
blanks.explanation: The moderate-demand branch of retail is 0.5 x 150 = 75, alongside the given 0.2 x 30 = 6 and 0.3 x 300 = 90.

blanks.placeholder: the EMV of the retail branch
blanks.explanation: Summing the weighted terms of the retail branch gives 6 + 75 + 90 = RM171,000.
The expected value selects the branch with the higher EMV, and retail at 171 beats online at 130, so the tree prunes the online branch.

blanks.placeholder: the expected return with perfect information
blanks.reveal: STATE AND WEIGHT IT: that EMV is 175
blanks.explanation: With perfect information the best payoff of each state is taken, 50 in low demand, 150 in medium and 300 in high, giving 10 + 75 + 90 = RM175,000.

blanks.placeholder: the EVPI in RM thousands
blanks.explanation: Value analysis compares the expected return with the information to the expected return without it: 175 - 171 = RM4,000, the most that demand research is worth.

steps: The tree reads from the decision on the left to the uncertain event, the level of demand, and out to the payoff of each branch, which is exactly the structure the chapter says a decision tree models, choices and uncertainties joined by branches.
The probabilities of the three states are 0.2, 0.5 and 0.3 and total 1, satisfying the requirement that the total probability of a complete set of outcomes must equal 1.

Each branch is weighted by multiplying every payoff by the probability of its state: online gives 0.2 x 50 + 0.5 x 120 + 0.3 x 200 = 10 + 60 + 60 = RM130,000, and retail gives 0.2 x 30 + 0.5 x 150 + 0.3 x 300 = 6 + 75 + 90 = RM171,000.

The expected value at the decision node is the best of those, so the retail branch is chosen at RM171,000 and the online branch is cut off, which is the risk-analysis treatment of uncertainty the chapter contrasts with certainty models and with uncertainty where probabilities are unknown.

Perfect information would let the firm take the best payoff of each state, 50, 150 and 300, for an expected return of 0.2 x 50 + 0.5 x 150 + 0.3 x 300 = 175, so the expected value of perfect information is 175 - 171 = RM4,000.

That RM4,000 is a ceiling price for demand forecasting: a study costing more than the increase in expected return is not worth buying, which is the comparison of expected return with and without the information that section 5.6 calls value analysis.

blanks.reveal: long-run frequency    relative frequency from enough history
blanks.explanation: With enough history an event's probability can be estimated by its relative frequency, which the chapter calls the long-run frequency route.
The subjective view holds that a probability represents an individual's degree of belief that an event will occur.
Direct probability forecasting simply asks an expert to estimate the chance that an outcome will occur.

blanks.placeholder: what odds forecasting proposes in series
blanks.reveal: odds               a series of bets tests the belief
blanks.explanation: Odds forecasting proposes a series of bets to determine how strongly the bettor feels that an event will occur.

blanks.placeholder: what kind of probabilities the one game has in comparison forecasting
blanks.reveal: comparison         like odds, but one game has known
blanks.explanation: Comparison forecasting is like odds forecasting except that one game has known probabilities, giving the bettor a reference point.

Sensitivity analysis says a variable is highly sensitive when a small change in its value yields a measurable change in output; variables that are not sensitive may be treated as fixed, reducing the model's complexity.

steps: The three requirements are the arithmetic every model in the chapter has to satisfy: each probability lies in the range 0 to 1, the probabilities of all outcomes of an event add up to the probability of their union, and a complete set of outcomes totals exactly 1.
Those requirements are what force a missing state of the economy to take the remainder, as with solid growth at 0.30 and stagnation at 0.45 leaving inflation at 0.25.

Section 5.5 then separates where the numbers come from: long-run frequency estimates a probability by relative frequency once there is enough history, the subjective view reads it as an individual's degree of belief, and a logic-derived probability may be sound but unacceptable in accuracy.

Section 5.6 elicits those estimates three ways, direct probability forecasting, which simply asks an expert for the chance, odds forecasting, which proposes a series of bets to measure the strength of feeling, and comparison forecasting, which is odds forecasting where one game has known probabilities.

Complex probabilities are decomposed instead of guessed, using conditional probabilities within subsets, so sales of a weather-related product are forecast under good weather and under bad weather and then combined with the probability of bad weather.

The model is finally tested rather than trusted: calibration asks whether 9 out of 10 of the 90% confidence intervals really land, most forecasters being too optimistic with intervals that are too tight, and sensitivity analysis flags any variable whose small change moves the output so that insensitive variables may be treated as fixed.

steps: The component block holds three items only: the action language, the display or presentation language and the knowledge base.

The five formats named under the action language - menu, question-answer, command language, input/output structured and free form - belong inside that one component, so they are not components themselves.
The middle block is the other list on the same slide: mental model, metaphors and idioms, navigation of the model and look are the modes of communication.

The last block separates three names learners often swap: the interface allows bidirectional communication, the GUI does it with icons and similar objects, and the UIMS is the DSS component handling all interaction between users and the system.

steps: The list in the first block is the closed set the chapter gives for basic action language types: menu, question-answer, command language, input/output structured and free form natural language.
Voice does not appear in that list, even though it is discussed later as a type of user interface - a distinction past-year papers like to test.

Each line in the second block pairs a saving with a cost: menus spare the user from learning commands but only suit simple systems, and once complexity grows several menu sets and sub menus are needed.

The question-answer type buys a natural dialogue but breaks down on unstructured answers, while the command-line type is powerful yet restricting, because the user actually has to learn the commands to make the system work.

steps: The first block contrasts the two process approaches: the life cycle's recursive phases from problem definition and feasibility analysis through implementation and maintenance, against prototyping, which follows the classic stages until the first prototype exists and then changes in small, constant steps.

Structure and discipline are what the life cycle buys, and rigidity is what it costs, which is why it is still often used today where the developer and the end users are in a contractual relationship.

ROMC analysis and functional category analysis are the two non-life-cycle approaches: one asks the developer to understand representations, operations, memory aids and controls, the other to pick the functions a specific DSS needs from a broad list of available functions.
The seven activities run in the order the chapter gives them, from problem diagnosis to incremental adaptation, and it notes that not all of them may be performed in every project.

Each activity has one signature phrase worth memorising: three categories of requirements at system analysis, components, structure and platform at system design, iterative prototyping at construction, and testing, evaluation and deployment at implementation.

The chapter's point is that a risk analysis run over these factors identifies several that may occur, and that identification calls for strategies to deal with them.

The lettered block is Alter's four general categories of implementation strategy, and the choice among them depends on available resources, the likelihood of project completion and the constraints specific to each strategy: A divides and evolves with prototypes and tools, B hides complexity and avoids change, C builds the support base, and D institutionalizes the system with training, mandatory use and tailoring to users' capabilities.

The last block is a different list again - the four measurement categories used to judge the finished DSS - so do not read it as part of the strategy set: system performance looks at response time, data entry, output format, usage and user interface, task performance at decision quality measured by time spent plus trust, confidence and satisfaction, business opportunities at development and operating costs, income and productivity, and evolutionary aspects at flexibility and overall functionality.

steps: The two definitions at the top are the ones papers trade over: a GDSS is a decision support system whose design, structure and usage reflect the way the members of a group interact to make a particular decision or type of decision, whereas groupware is only software providing collaborative support to groups, with different time and place applications and most of it built on Internet technologies.

The characteristics block adds what the GDSS is said to allow: members located in different places and working at different times, information located external to the project, and rapid solutions - while still exhibiting the normal team problems of synergy or conflict, and going by the names computer-supported cooperative work or collaborative computing.

The levels block is the chapter's ladder of collaboration capability, from collected work as uncoordinated individual efforts (sprinters), through coordinated work as coordinated individual efforts (relay), up to concerted work as a concerted team effort (crew), with the degree of collaborative effort rising as you go down the list.

The benefits and problems block keeps the vocabulary tight: groupwork pays off in process gains, illustrated by the nominal group technique and the Delphi method and by hardware and software combined as GDSS, while groupwork that fails is recorded as process losses and called inefficient.

The final block is the order of the standard meeting process, and it is the same order the meeting slides tell as a story: participants brainstorm by entering comments, the facilitator runs idea organization software to sort those comments into common themes, the results are displayed, themes are prioritized, and the highest priority topics are either sent through the process again or put to a vote before the final idea is selected.
